title: Salsa: NOT THE DANCE
summary: Josh and Chuck explore salsa as a condiment: its origins in Mesoamerica thousands of years ago, the Aztec-era sauce descriptions recorded by Bernardino de Sahagún, the 1571 Spanish dictionary entry for "salsa," early European recipes, and the Mexican-American spread of salsa in Texas and the Southwest. They cover David Pace's Pace Picante brand and its 1980s-90s ad campaigns, salsa outselling ketchup, tortilla chip origins (Elmer Doolan, the El Zarepta factory, and Jose Bartolome Martinez, the "Corn King of San Antonio"), and the chips-and-salsa tradition. They then survey salsa styles (pico de gallo, chipotle, salsa verde, salsa macha, and Peruvian and Ecuadorian "criolla"), distinguish salsa from mole and hot sauce, and end with a listener email about a great-grandmother's 1930s custody hearing.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and salsa definition
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the show intro and the pronunciation of salsa, and note that salsa became America's favorite condiment, outselling ketchup. They discuss how Mexican salsa is a condiment, not a sauce, and compare eating chips with salsa to other food habits.

segments.title: Ancient origins of salsa in Mesoamerica
segments.summary: Salsa-like mixtures of chilies and tomatoes date back nine or ten thousand years in Mesoamerica. Bernardino de Sahagún's Florentine Codex describes many Aztec market sauces. The mocajete lava-rock mortar is mentioned. Tomatoes are indigenous to Mesoamerica, and chilies were misnamed peppers by Columbus. The word salsa was a generic Spanish word for sauce, and a 1571 Spanish dictionary listed it as an Aztec-style tomato chili condiment.

segments.title: Early European reception and Columbian exchange
segments.summary: Europeans initially thought tomatoes were toxic, a nightshade relative. Antonio Latini wrote one of the first recipes resembling salsa, called Spanish-style tomato sauce. Discussion of Columbian exchange foods such as garlic, cilantro, and onions, and the use of fats in Mexican cooking.

segments.title: Salsa vs mole and hot sauce
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish salsa from mole, which is a smooth sauce with many ingredients and is drenched over dishes, and from hot sauce, which originated in Massachusetts in the early 1800s and is typically chili, vinegar, and salt.

segments.title: Chips and salsa in the American Southwest
segments.summary: Much of the American Southwest was once Mexican territory, and Mexican food thrived there. Tex-Mex and Cal-Mex were born from a blend of Mexican and American cuisines. A 1934 LA Times recipe for chili salsa is cited.

segments.title: David Pace and Pace Picante
segments.summary: David Pace, a Louisiana native from a molasses bottling family, settled in San Antonio and created Pace Picante sauce, which made tomato the star. His son-in-law Kit Goldsberry took the brand to the mainstream in the late 1970s and 1980s, with a fat-free health trend helping sales. The 1989 'New York City' ad and the 1993 'Get a rope' ad from a Camp Cowboy commercial featuring Ralph Bonzo Bear Stedman are discussed.

segments.title: Salsa outselling ketchup and tortilla chips history
segments.summary: The hosts marvel that salsa outsold ketchup, which happened in 1991 and was overtaken in 1996. Tortilla chip origins are discussed: Elmer Doolan and Fritos, the El Zarape tortilla factory in LA in the 1940s that cut misshapen tortillas into chips, and Jose Bartolome Martinez, the Corn King of San Antonio, who set up industrial corn mills and produced tortilla chips in the 1910s.

segments.title: Origins of free chips and salsa at restaurants
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the tradition of free chips and salsa at Mexican restaurants and whether charging for it is off-putting. A Reddit historian traced the possible first restaurant serving chips with salsa to Machaos or El Nido in Phoenix in the early to mid 1970s, which had earlier served hot sauce on chips.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Brief transition to a break before the sauce styles section.

segments.title: Types of salsa: pico de gallo, chipotle, salsa verde, salsa macha
segments.summary: The hosts describe pico de gallo, which means rooster's beak, along with salsa de chile chipotle, salsa verde made with tomatillos, and salsa macha from Veracruz made with dried chilies, peanuts, sesame, oil and vinegar. Trader Joe's and Mátido's jarred salsa verde are mentioned. Salsa criolla, from Peru and Ecuador, and chimichurri are discussed as non-Mexican variants.

segments.title: Lafonda restaurant and East Lake Garden shout-out
segments.summary: The hosts praise the free table-side salsa at Lafonda in Atlanta. Josh mentions a Lafonda near him and the East Lake Garden community garden, plus a sign painted by local artist Ronnie.

segments.title: Listener mail: Tamara's great-grandmother Judida
segments.summary: A listener named Tamara shares a story about her great-grandmother Judida, an Italian immigrant in 1930s Pennsylvania whose husband was hurt in a coal mining accident. She negotiated with a judge in Italian to keep her children by receiving state money to care for them herself.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank Tamara, note her grandmother is alive at 97, invite listener emails, and close the episode.
